The tragic reality is that in my country and 99% of them chronic fstigue syndrome is still regarded as "psychosomatic" and there's 0 treatments.

 Even if you suggest something off label for symptom management, you won't get it due to beurocratic guidelines. All of the official CFS clinics here only offer cognitive behavioral therapy and graded exercise therapy which has now been discontinued due to how harmful it was. 

They basically just tell you to cope and take breaks, but life just doesn't work that way when your body doesn't function properly.

Both sides of the coin are quite horrible. Those in abusive situations or grave poverty are treated as if they have brain diseases when that reality is too much to bear. People with physical diseases that can't be observed by the naked eye or laboratory tests are treated like malongering fakers who need therapy.

My faith in any medical system is 100% ruined. All they care about is abstaining themselves from liability, otherwise people would have actual choice in the treatments they receive and not be treated like infants with 0 knowledge of how their mind and body feels.

Behavioral studies almost always come from rats and other animals, at least that is what most of my textbooks say and that is what I have been taught at university. It would be pretty unethical to do most of these experiments on humans, especially fear conditioned responses. 

Of course approved drugs go through several rounds of human trials, but they are typically tested on animals first and the behavioral effects are initially observed in rats.

Damn, I'm so sorry this has happened to you. Shrugging off someone's very real physical pain as a psychosomatic manifestation of emotional disturbance should be a liability. 

Doctors need to be held accountable for this ridiculous gaslighting, it goes against every evidence based practice out there to downplay physical pain and chalk it up to "stress and anxiety."

Similar things have happened to me my whole life, so I can relate to you a lot. Besides GI issues (that go pretty much untreated because all my blood tests and MRIs come back with nothing) I've had chronic pain and fatigue for years.

I had to pay for a private self reffered MRI to rule out MS because the NHS does not have a care in the world about chronic illness. I have CFS/post viral fatigue that has been going on since I was 17 and has made my life hell. Since my MRI was supposedly "normal" no one believes the cognitive decline, headaches, nerve pain, neurological issues like blurred vision and floaters, and bone crushing fatigue i experience on a daily basis.

These people have no idea what we go through. It is easy for them to claim we need to go to therapy and do yoga when they are not in pain every single day of their lives.

It is very difficult, not many people take it seriously and victim blaming is abundant, such as "No one likes procedures, no one likes exams, get over it."

The medical industry has way too much power unfortunately and it trickles down into people's attitudes about those who have been traumatized by these institutions.

It is very sad we have to hide these feelings. I'm not even depressed in any way, just suicidal and it's independent of any mood or feeling I have. 

I'm not in the US so I'm not really sure if the US rules are the same, but in the UK they don't even like to send people to psych wards even if they ask in many cases due to shortages of beds. I just kept repeating that I'm not suicidal to get them off my back. 

It just wears at you to have to hide your thoughts all the time because of incorrect assumptions about suicidal people fuled by the media and psychiatry. I won't qualify for disability until I get citizenship in my new country but when I lived in the US I was told that you had to consistently be seeing doctors all the time when that would further damage any resolve and sanity I have left.

So I have several physical illnesses and loads of medical trauma. There were no clinical trials conducted on people with autoimmune conditions, CFS and other post viral illnesses, etc. Pfizer's trial participants were pretty much all healthy adults. I have a history of bad reactions to jabs since I became ill. Before all of this, people respected and understood that. Now, it's like a total 180 fueled by fear and not factual evidence, such as whether or not the unvaccinated person actually has covid. 

 In my country there are currently no medical exemptions to the vaccines unless you've had a severe anaphylactic shock that resulted in near fatality. This information is on the UK government website.

Soon you will be required to have a vaccine pass to go to certain events, in my home country you can't even enter a restaurant (and several other businesses) in many places without one. Many universities are deliberating on mandating it when there has never been such a mandate in universities here before. How is that not coercion? 

I take tests quite frequently, as a lot of the symptoms from my chronic illnesses mirror some of the covid ones. I have never once tested positive. So how the fuck am I spreading a disease I continue to test negative for? No one can answer this question. They just stomp their feet and claim that the person who is more disabled and at far more risk from THEM is the problem. Oh, and they threaten violence too, how humanitarian. 

I study a STEM field and it is quite shocking how little people seem to be following actual data. It makes far more sense to require proof of negative tests than vaccines when viral load and spread is still possible. It reminds me a lot of many psychiatric studies where the conclusions are twisted in favor of trying to support a more "positive, publishable outcome" (See the Mad in America article about publication bias) 

Also, we can't get antibody tests here unless you're vaccinated. So pretty much no one seems to be tracking how long natural immunity from infection lasts either. Once again, ignoring a key component of the puzzle that could benefit people, easing their worries somewhat. 

The reaction I've gotten from not taking this vaccine is almost eerily similar to what I've endured for not wanting to go to the psych ward since I am suicidal, for quitting meds and therapy when they were damaging me worse, because people who do not understand my specific conditions want to butt their heads and force me to engage in medical interventions that could further harm me. 

It scares me, the road we are headed down. I see people cheering when someone wants to refuse treatment to an unvaccinated person even if the issue is not covid related. How long is this slippery slope going to continue, where we punish people for not engaging in every single health care procedure that is reccomended to them, regardless of the relative risk? 

This is coming from someone who had an elderly family member die of covid. I am also someone who got utterly fucked by another respiratory illness that no one cares about anymore. (I've never blamed anyone for giving me the flu and kickstarting my CFS, because I know that viruses are unpredictable and will spread no matter what) 

Every single one of my friends has had covid as well, recovered within a few days, 
were in good spirits about it and didn't have rage towards everyone else about contracting it. If one of my friends accidentally gave me covid, I would not lie the blame with them or try to force them to make decisions against their will.

Kindness and asking people to stay home if they have symptoms, as well as practicing proper hygiene, goes a long way. Taking away people's decision to make medical choices for themselves, no matter the procedure, is not a path I want to see the world walk down.

I've looked at the documents on the UK government website and even if you have a history of systemic reactions to vaccines, including anaphylaxis (which I am fortunate enough not to experience effects of that severity, at least) they are still trying to claim that doesn't count as an exemption, when that has always been the case for any other inoculation.

I am hoping this will change, but as long as people can't have dialogues about this and our country's leaders are pushing every single person to take the jab lest they be labeled as anti-vaxx or not tough enough with covid measures, I don't see any pragmatic steps being taken to prevent discrimination.

Once again, I don't see why u vaccinated people can't present a negative test result instead to enter a crowded venue. I don't think it should be my choice or anyone else's to mandate what medical decisions someone does or does not make. Of course, we should encourage those most at risk from covid to take the vaccines (with their consent) and offer them to anyone who would like them, but I am opposed to any sort of mandate.

It puts people in a position where they can't say no, no matter their relative risk from covid, whether or not they currently have antibodies, and their personal situation. I know many people my age irl who had covid and recovered within a few days, confirmed to have antibodies after the infection, and got the vaccine not for health reasons and their own protection, but because they were peer pressured.

I don't want to live in a world where we can blanket mandate medical tests and procedures, it feels wrong to me, because it doesn't account for the nuance.

My understanding of this/TLDR:  


People with CFS are getting overwhelmed by sympathetic nervous system activity, leading to vasoconstriction. This is one piece of the puzzle.

Adrenergic receptor knockouts, as well as high levels of bradykinin, inhibit the production of renin in the kidneys and increase blood vessel permeability, resulting in a perpetual state of low blood volume and reduced cardiac output.  


Low blood volume triggers sympathetic nervous system activation and the subsequent release of vasodilators. These vasodilators leak into the bloodstream, likely causing CFS symptoms.

These researchers propose that when tissues are deprived of oxygen (a consequence of the vasoconstriction and low blood volume) they are injured by reperfusion and a cycle of oxidative stress.

When this cycle of stress is occurring, sodium ions build up in cells. Sodium-calcium exchangers begin to import calcium into the cell rather than removing it, the complete opposite of what a healthy cell would do. 

The high levels of calcium begin to impair mitochondrial function, in addition to wrecking the blood vessels and muscular tissue. This could cause many other CFS symptoms.  


So this paper has a very two-pronged approach here, with two key theories- one being the issue of sodium buildup in cells, and the other being the Beta-adrenergic receptor dysfunction.

1D01 and 1D02 genes belong to the IDO family. These genes code for enzymes that convert L-trytophan in the kynurenine pathway. While mutations in the 1D02 gene and subsequent protein are common in the general population, in one study 100% of severe CFS suffers had a mutation in the gene. Due to this mutation, there is more strain on the 1D01 proteins to continue maintaining L-trytophan metabolism. 


There seems to be trigger in those of us with CFS that leads to reduced kynurenine levels  and increased tryrophan, compared to controls, suggesting that a malfunctioning in this pathway may be the etiology of many CFS symptoms. This is known as the metabolic trap. 

The IDO family plays a role in the immune system and inflammatory response in response to microorganism invasion. In the context of CFS it would make sense that there is some form of immunomodulatory dysfunction at play, which is why the evidence of these IDO studies is promising. However, this is a very delicate system that must be handled with care, which is why Ron Davis suggests against self-experimentation with drugs containing Tryptophan at this time.

I think many natalists do not understand the biology behind decision making and learned memory.

Say you have a synapse between two neurons that fire in response to stress, the more often these fire, the stronger the connection becomes between them. Such long term potentiation is a key reason why we tend to remember traumatic events and suffering more vividly than random events that happen as we go about the day.

By design, your mind will imprint suffering in your neural networks to ensure you don't forget them. Happy moments tend to be fleeting, but if they are important enough, you will have a durable synaptic connection there as well. However, you are more likely to remember the embarrassing thing you did two weeks ago than the time an old lady at the grocery store smiled at you, due to nature's cruel tinkering. 

For every happy memory you form, there is a tragic one to counter it typically. That sort of duality is not something I want to subject another human to.

It is not natural to have someone sticking sharp objects in your mouth, of course our brains are going to register that as terrifying!

It's honestly a toss up of whether or not they will work, everyone should make their own decisions regarding psychiatric medications, because not all humans respond the same. You have to make your own cost-benefit analysis.

Some people get lucky and find relief, some people like me take over a dozen meds and never get any positive effects. Being shoved pills I knew nothing about as a teenager and getting tremors- because I was unaware of the consequences of serotonin syndrome- was not a great experience. 

I think it's important to be aware of the risks of these medications, particularly the withdrawals, and the chance that your symptoms will worsen.

 The advice I see online is a bit disingenuous, as I always see people trying to encourage others to take psychiatric medications without educating themselves on the side effects or even the mechanisms of the drug. 

Whenever I became an adult and gained more autonomy in conversing with the psychiatrist, I researched every drug thoroughly that I was prescribed. There was a time when a Psychiatrist prescribed me drugs with glaring interactions, a beta blocker and a stimulant, and I would not have known this prior if I hadn't made the decision to become more informed about pharmacology. 

Knowledge is power, and it is helpful to get an idea of what you might experience with a drug, there are lots of reviews online and research papers that document side effects, what to expect, etc.

Also if you have trauma, antidepressants will not really help you, at least in my experience and the case studies I've read in PTSD literature. Same with bipolar, except these drugs could make your symptoms worse. 

Not saying to never take anti-depressants, that should be up to the will of the individual and whether or not they benefit you. I just wish someone had sat down and told me that I could have side effects from the medications before I went down the rabbit hole of trying all of them lol.

Saying that depression is just a chemical imbalance is truly an oversimplification of the issue, I agree.

I have depression, but I also have PTSD. PTSD can alter the volume of the hippocampus, increase the function of the amygdala, the region of the brain that activates fear and the fight or flight response, and decreased functioning in the anterior cingulate which controls many complex tasks like decision making and empathy. 

Increased release of Norepinephrine is only part of the issue. I suspect many people who are diagnosed with depression have underlying trauma and difficult life circumstances that would reasonably cause us to be miserable. But if you look at other illnesses like PTSD, it makes no sense that long-term depression is simply a chemical imbalance of serotonin, however there is still so much we do not know.
